blocks.text: MRI uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to produce detailed images of internal structures. Its principle is that tissues contain different amounts of hydrogen atoms, which have magnetic properties.

items: Procedure: the patient lies on a motorised table that slides into a large tube-like scanner containing a powerful magnet. Radio waves make the hydrogen atoms in the body give off signals, which a receiver detects; a computer builds a detailed three-dimensional image.
Uses: imaging soft tissues such as the brain, spinal cord and internal organs, and finding abnormalities in blood vessels and certain tumours.

blocks.alt: Three panels. EEG: a head with electrodes on the scalp wired to an amplifier, and five wave traces labelled gamma, beta, alpha, theta and delta from fastest to slowest. CT: a ring-shaped gantry round a patient on a table, an X-ray tube at the top that rotates round the patient and detectors opposite. MRI: a tube-shaped scanner with a powerful magnet round a patient on a table, and radio waves that make hydrogen atoms give signals.
blocks.caption: Magnetic resonance imaging (original diagram after the second Figure 15.23).
blocks.long_description: EEG records the brain's electrical activity: electrodes on the scalp pick up signals, an amplifier magnifies them and they are shown as waves; it is painless and used for seizures, epilepsy and tumours. A CT scan sends X-rays from a tube rotating round the patient; detectors measure how much each tissue absorbs and a computer builds cross-sectional images. MRI uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves: hydrogen atoms in the tissues give signals that a computer turns into detailed three-dimensional images, especially of soft tissues such as the brain and spinal cord.
